quick.title: Quick Practice
quick.description: Five short situational-judgement questions across five core capabilities. Doesn't count toward your formal skill passport.

full.title: Full Capability Assessment
full.description: A comprehensive, timed assessment covering all twelve capability domains. Counts toward your formal skill passport.

items.background: You were meant to hand a client file to a colleague before end of day, but you forgot. They find out from the client the next morning.

options.A: Tell your colleague and the client directly what happened, and fix it immediately.
options.B: Apologise to your colleague, then quietly finish the handover.
options.C: Wait to see if your colleague raises it before saying anything.
options.D: Explain that you were busy with other priorities.

items.background: Two people ask for your help at the same time, both say it's urgent, and you can only do one before your next commitment.
items.text: How do you decide what to do?

options.A: Quickly ask both what the actual deadline and impact is, then choose based on that.
options.B: Help whoever asked first.
options.C: Help whoever seems more senior or important.
options.D: Try to do a bit of both and hope it's enough.

items.background: A project you're responsible for will be a week late. You need to tell the person relying on it.
items.text: What does your message focus on?

options.A: The reason for the delay, the new date, and what you're doing so it doesn't happen again.
options.B: Just the new date, to keep it brief.
options.C: A general apology without specifics.
options.D: Waiting until they ask before saying anything.

items.background: You're working on a group task and disagree with the approach a teammate wants to take.

options.A: Raise your concern directly with them and ask to talk through both approaches.
options.B: Go along with it to avoid conflict.
options.C: Mention it to another teammate first to see if they agree.
options.D: Do it your own way without saying anything.

items.background: A report shows a result that doesn't match what you expected, and a decision is waiting on it.
items.text: What do you do before acting on the report?

options.A: Check the underlying data and assumptions before treating it as fact.
options.B: Assume the report is right since it's already been produced.
options.C: Ask someone else to double-check it instead of you.
options.D: Go with your original expectation instead.

items.background: You'd prepared for a group presentation, but the format changes to something different the night before.

options.A: Recheck what's actually required now and adjust your prep to fit the new format.
options.B: Present largely what you prepared and hope it still fits.
options.C: Tell the group you're not ready and ask to go last.
options.D: Feel frustrated and put in minimal extra effort since it changed at the last minute.

items.background: You've failed the same practical task twice despite following the instructions you were given.

options.A: Ask someone experienced to watch you attempt it and point out what you're missing.
options.B: Try again exactly the same way, hoping it works this time.
options.C: Avoid the task and focus on things you're already good at.
options.D: Decide it's not for you and stop trying.

items.background: You're asked to complete a task using software or an app you've never used before, with a deadline today.

options.A: Spend a few minutes exploring its basic functions or checking a help guide before starting.
options.B: Ask someone else to do it for you instead.
options.C: Start clicking around and hope you figure it out as you go.
options.D: Avoid the task and say you can't do it because you don't know the tool.

items.background: You find information online that would support an assignment or task, but you're not sure how reliable the source is.
items.text: What do you do before using it?

options.A: Check the source and cross-reference it against at least one other reliable source.
options.B: Use it since it was the first result that looked relevant.
options.C: Use it but mention you're not sure it's accurate.
options.D: Use it without checking, since it's easier.

items.situation_title: A big task, a tight deadline
items.background: You're given a task with several steps and two weeks to finish it.

options.A: Break it into steps, estimate how long each will take, and schedule them across the two weeks.
options.B: Start immediately on the first thing that comes to mind.
options.C: Wait until you have a clearer picture before starting anything.
options.D: Leave it until closer to the deadline, since two weeks feels like plenty of time.

items.background: You realise two things you're responsible for are due on the same day, and you only noticed a few days out.

options.A: Look at both immediately, work out what's realistic, and flag early if one might slip.
options.B: Focus only on whichever one you personally find more interesting.
options.C: Start both at once without a clear plan for either.
options.D: Hope you can finish both without changing how you're currently working.

items.background: While doing a repetitive task, you notice a way it could be done faster or better than the way you were shown.

options.A: Try it and, once you've confirmed it works, share it with whoever else does the task.
options.B: Keep using the better way yourself, but don't mention it to anyone.
options.C: Keep doing it the original way since that's what you were shown.
options.D: Mention it once in passing but don't follow up either way.

items.background: You notice something that needs doing but nobody has been formally assigned to it.

options.A: Raise it and offer to take it on, or find out who should.
options.B: Assume someone else will notice and deal with it.
options.C: Mention it to a friend but not to anyone who could act on it.
options.D: Ignore it since it's not your job.

items.background: You could take credit for work a group member did, or claim you completed something you didn't finish, and it's unlikely anyone would find out.

options.A: Represent the work accurately, including what you didn't finish or didn't do yourself.
options.B: Let the ambiguity stand without correcting it, but don't actively lie if asked.
options.C: Imply you did more than you did if it's not directly asked.
options.D: Take the credit since it's unlikely to be checked.

items.background: You notice someone has made an honest but significant error that could affect others, and pointing it out might be awkward.

options.A: Raise it directly and privately with the person, focused on fixing it.
options.B: Mention it to someone else and let them decide whether to raise it.
options.C: Say nothing unless it's specifically asked about.
options.D: Say nothing, since it's not your responsibility.

items.background: You're comparing two options and one claims to be "50% faster" than the other, based on a small, informal test.
items.text: How do you treat that claim?

options.A: Treat it as a rough indication, and check what it was actually measured against before relying on it.
options.B: Accept it as accurate, since it's stated as a specific number.
options.C: Ignore the number entirely and decide on gut feeling instead.
options.D: Repeat the claim to others without mentioning it might be rough.

items.background: You're shown a chart with two trend lines that cross over partway through, and asked which option has performed better recently.

options.A: Focus on the recent section specifically, since "recently" is what was asked, not the whole chart.
options.B: Answer based on which line is higher on average across the whole chart.
options.C: Guess based on which line looks bigger overall.
options.D: Say you can't tell anything from a chart.

items.background: You're not sure what your next step should be after your current course, job, or stage of study.

options.A: Seek out information and advice — from a mentor, careers service, or people already doing it — and compare a few real options.
options.B: Wait until someone tells you what you should do next.
options.C: Pick the first option that comes up without comparing it to anything else.
options.D: Avoid thinking about it until you're forced to decide.

items.background: You receive feedback on your work or performance that's more critical than you expected.

options.A: Ask a clarifying question so you understand specifically what to do differently.
options.B: Accept it politely but don't follow up on what it actually means for you.
options.C: Feel discouraged and avoid the topic afterwards.
options.D: Dismiss it as unfair without considering it.

items.background: A project you contributed to as part of a group fails to meet its target, partly due to a mistake you made.
items.text: How do you respond when the group discusses what happened?

options.A: Name your part in it clearly, without minimising it or blaming others for your share.
options.B: Acknowledge it only if someone else brings it up first.
options.C: Focus mainly on what other people got wrong.
options.D: Stay quiet and hope it isn't traced back to you.

items.background: You need to make a decision today, but you don't have all the information you'd like, and getting it would take longer than you have.

options.A: Decide based on the best available information, and note the assumption you're making.
options.B: Delay the decision past the deadline until you have everything.
options.C: Ask someone else to make the call instead.
options.D: Pick randomly since you don't have enough information anyway.

items.background: You need to explain a decision or a result to someone who doesn't have the same background knowledge as you.

options.A: Explain it in plain terms first, then add detail if they want it.
options.B: Explain it exactly as you'd explain it to a peer with the same background.
options.C: Give a very short answer and let them ask if they need more.
options.D: Avoid the topic since it would take too long to explain properly.

items.background: You're part of a small group task, and one person hasn't contributed anything so far, with the deadline approaching.

options.A: Check in with them directly to understand what's going on and agree on what they'll do.
options.B: Quietly do their share yourself so the group isn't affected.
options.C: Complain about them to the rest of the group without talking to them.
options.D: Say nothing and let the group's result suffer.

items.background: Two people you trust give you conflicting advice about the same decision.

options.A: Ask each of them what their advice is based on, then weigh the reasoning, not just who said it.
options.B: Go with whoever you spoke to most recently.
options.C: Go with whoever is more senior or experienced by default.
options.D: Avoid deciding and hope the situation resolves itself.
